concepts.label: Propranolol is used to treat essential tremor, including in elderly patients
concepts.definition: Essential tremor is a common movement disorder causing a fine, bilateral action/postural tremor of the hands, distinct from the resting tremor of Parkinson disease. Propranolol, a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist, is first-line pharmacological therapy: blocking peripheral beta-2 receptors in skeletal muscle reduces the tremor's amplitude. It is used across age groups, including elderly patients, though beta-blockade requires caution in comorbidities such as bradycardia, asthma or decompensated heart failure.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that propranolol is used to treat essential tremor.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing propranolol's use for essential tremor (an action/postural tremor, beta-blocker first-line) with its separate, already-covered use as a comparator to amitriptyline in migraine prophylaxis, or with the resting tremor of Parkinson disease, which is not first-line treated with propranolol.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 6 ("propranolol / Case: BPH, old, Tremors"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf, p1.

concepts.label: Anterior spinal artery occlusion at the spinal cord level causes bilateral flaccid paraplegia below the lesion with bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, sparing the dorsal columns
concepts.article_title: Anterior spinal artery syndrome at the spinal cord level
concepts.definition: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord (the corticospinal, spinothalamic tracts and anterior horns), while the paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns. Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery at the spinal cord level (anterior spinal artery/anterior cord syndrome) therefore causes bilateral motor weakness (flaccid initially, becoming spastic paraplegia below the lesion) and bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion, while proprioception and vibration sense (carried by the dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries) are classically spared. This spinal cord-level syndrome is distinct from medial medullary syndrome, in which anterior spinal artery territory occlusion at the medulla produces the different, more localised picture of ipsilateral tongue weakness with contralateral limb weakness.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that anterior spinal artery occlusion at the spinal cord level causes bilateral paraplegia with bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, sparing the dorsal columns.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing spinal cord-level anterior spinal artery occlusion (bilateral deficits below the lesion, dorsal columns spared) with medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery territory occlusion at the medulla, producing ipsilateral tongue weakness and contralateral limb weakness/proprioceptive loss instead).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 10 ("Anterior spinal / Bilateral paraplegia And loss of pain and temp... Asa occlusion"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 10 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf (src_9bf95afe8820539ea286), p2.

concepts.label: Naloxone, a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist, is used to reverse fentanyl (opioid) intoxication
concepts.definition: Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at the mu-opioid receptor, given intravenously or intramuscularly to acutely reverse opioid intoxication/overdose, restoring respiratory drive and consciousness within minutes. Because it is short-acting relative to many opioids (including the potent, high-affinity opioid fentanyl), repeated doses or an infusion may be needed to prevent re-sedation as naloxone wears off before the opioid does. This acute reversal role is distinct from naltrexone, a related but long-acting oral antagonist used for relapse prevention after detoxification, not for acute overdose.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that naloxone is used to acutely reverse fentanyl (opioid) intoxication.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing naloxone (short-acting, parenteral, used for acute overdose reversal) with naltrexone (long-acting, oral, used for relapse prevention after detoxification) — both are mu-opioid antagonists but serve different clinical roles.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 19 ("Naloxone / Fentanyl intoxication"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 19 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf (src_9bf95afe8820539ea286), p3.

concepts.label: The cochlear nucleus is the origin of the trapezoid body
concepts.article_title: The cochlear nucleus as the origin of the trapezoid body
concepts.definition: The trapezoid body is a bundle of decussating auditory fibres in the ventral pons, part of the ascending central auditory pathway. Its fibres arise from the (ventral) cochlear nucleus, the first central relay station for auditory information after the cochlear nerve; many of these fibres cross the midline within the trapezoid body to reach the contralateral superior olivary nucleus and, ultimately, the inferior colliculus, underpinning the bilateral, partially crossed representation of sound needed for binaural hearing and sound localisation.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the cochlear nucleus is the origin of the trapezoid body.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the trapezoid body's origin (the cochlear nucleus) with its destination structures (the superior olivary nucleus, which it synapses upon after decussating, and the inferior colliculus further along the pathway).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 22 ("Cochlear nucleus / Origine of trapezoid"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 22 of EOM - paper 1 cns 2020.pdf (src_9bf95afe8820539ea286), p3.
